short: Lecture 14 · Life satisfaction and depression in married women
note: This article's licence doesn't allow it to be republished on this website, so its text isn't shown here.
Open your Lecture 14 PDF (Article 1: Srivastava, 2016) next to this page and answer the tasks from it.

Where things are in the PDF: Abstract; I. Introduction (definitions of life satisfaction and depression, then the literature review); II. Methodology (aim, objectives, hypotheses); III. Tools used; IV. Procedure (sample, inclusion and exclusion criteria); V. Statistical analysis; VI. Result (two correlation tables on page 6); VII. Discussion; VIII. Conclusion; Limitation; Future direction.

items.label: Aim
items.prompt: What is the aim of the study? (Section II)
items.model: To see the relationship between life satisfaction and depression among working and non-working married women.
items.why: The aim and the objective are worded almost the same. It's a relationship (correlational) aim, not a cause-and-effect one.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Look at the hypothesis in Section II, then at how the Discussion describes it. What do you notice?
options: Both sections state the same directional hypothesis in almost the same words
The Method's hypothesis has no direction, but the Discussion reports a directional one
No hypothesis is stated anywhere, only an aim and an objective in Section II
Both predict a difference in depression between working and non-working women
items.ans: The Method's hypothesis has no direction, but the Discussion reports a directional one
items.model: Method: 'There will be significant relationship…' (no direction). Discussion: 'higher levels of depression would be associated with reduced life satisfaction' (direction).
items.why: The hypothesis you test must be the one you stated BEFORE the data. Changing it afterwards is a red flag.

items.label: Variables
items.prompt: Which TWO variables are correlated, and what is the grouping variable?
items.model: Life satisfaction and depression are correlated; working vs non-working status splits the sample into two groups.
items.why: In a correlational study neither variable is truly an IV. Working status is a grouping (subject) variable, not manipulated.

items.label: Research design
items.prompt: Which best describes the design?
options: A true experiment in which employment status was manipulated by the researcher
A cross-sectional correlational study carried out separately in two groups
A longitudinal study following the same married women over several years
A case study describing a small number of depressed working women in depth
items.ans: A cross-sectional correlational study carried out separately in two groups
items.model: Cross-sectional correlational study.
items.why: Questionnaires given once, correlations computed separately for working and non-working women. Nothing manipulated.

items.label: Sampling method
items.prompt: How were the participants selected?
options: Simple random sampling from a population list
Stratified random sampling by employment status
Purposive sampling (a non-probability method)
Snowball sampling through participants' friends
items.model: Purposive (non-probability) sampling.
items.why: 'Selected purposively'. Non-probability samples limit generalisation to all working/non-working married women.

items.label: Sample size
items.prompt: How many participants in total, and how many in each group?
items.model: 140 married women: 70 working and 70 non-working.
items.why: With n = 70 per group, only moderate-or-larger correlations are likely to reach significance.

items.label: Inclusion / exclusion criteria
items.prompt: What is the main problem with the inclusion and exclusion criteria?
options: They are far too strict, so very few married women in the area were eligible
They overlap, and never require participants to be married or define 'working'
They wrongly exclude women over 30, which shrinks the age range of the sample
They are not reported at all, so the reader cannot tell who could take part
items.ans: They overlap, and never require participants to be married or define 'working'
items.model: Redundant criteria, and the key features of the sample (married; working vs not) aren't defined.
items.why: Criteria should define exactly who can be in the study. 'Females having any organisity' is also vague and undefined.

items.label: Operational definition: life satisfaction
items.prompt: How was LIFE SATISFACTION measured? (Name the scale and its developer.)
items.model: Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al.), 5 items about overall evaluation of one's life.
items.why: The operational definition = the score on this scale.

items.label: Operational definition: depression
items.prompt: How was DEPRESSION measured?
items.model: Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II): 21-item self-report inventory.
items.why: Note the tools list calls it 'Back's Depression Inventory': a careless error that weakens credibility.

items.label: Reliability and validity
items.prompt: Does the article report reliability (e.g. Cronbach's α) for the scales in THIS sample?
options: Yes, Cronbach's alpha is reported for both scales in this sample
Only for the BDI-II, taken from the original 1996 test manual
No, neither reliability nor validity evidence is reported here
Yes, test-retest reliability over two weeks is reported for both
items.ans: No, neither reliability nor validity evidence is reported here
items.model: No reliability or validity evidence is given.
items.why: Compare with the Instagram article, which reports Cronbach's α for every scale. Without it we can't judge measurement quality.

items.label: Statistical analysis
items.prompt: What statistical analysis was used to test the hypothesis?
items.model: Pearson correlation (plus means and SDs), using SPSS version 16.
items.why: Correlation fits a relationship hypothesis. Note that no test COMPARES the two groups.

items.label: Result: working women
items.prompt: From the first results table, give r and p for WORKING married women.
items.model: r = −.079, p = .517: NOT significant.
items.why: p > .05, so there is no significant relationship for working women.

items.label: Result: non-working women
items.prompt: From the second table, give r and p for NON-WORKING married women.
items.model: r = −.325, p = .006: significant, weak-to-moderate negative correlation.
items.why: Higher depression goes with lower life satisfaction among non-working women. r² ≈ .11, so about 11% shared variance.

items.label: Do the results support the abstract?
items.prompt: The abstract says there is a 'significant relationship between life satisfaction and depression among working and non-working married women'. Is that accurate?
options: Yes, because both correlations in the results tables are statistically significant
No: only the non-working group's correlation is significant; working women's is not
No: neither group's correlation reaches significance at the .05 level in the tables
Yes, because the correlation for the combined sample of 140 women is significant
items.ans: No: only the non-working group's correlation is significant; working women's is not
items.model: Only the non-working group's correlation is significant.
items.why: This is the biggest flaw: the conclusion overclaims and ignores a non-significant result in their own table.

items.label: Wrong group in the Discussion
items.prompt: In the Discussion, the authors describe the finding as being 'among married and unmarried working women'. What's wrong?
options: Nothing: it correctly describes the two groups of women who were actually studied
The study had no unmarried women: it compared working vs non-working married women
The study only included unmarried women, so 'married' is the incorrect word there
It should say working men, because men were also included in the final sample
items.ans: The study had no unmarried women: it compared working vs non-working married women
items.model: The Discussion describes a sample that wasn't studied.
items.why: Always check that the Discussion talks about the same sample and variables as the Method.

items.label: Comparing the groups
items.prompt: The title implies a comparison between working and non-working women. Did the authors statistically compare the two groups?
options: Yes, with a t-test
Yes, by testing the difference between the two correlations
No: they only computed a separate correlation for each group
Yes, with ANOVA
items.ans: No: they only computed a separate correlation for each group
items.model: No group comparison was tested.
items.why: To claim the groups differ you would need e.g. a t-test on mean depression/life satisfaction or a test of the difference between the two r values.

items.label: Conclusion
items.prompt: The Conclusion says depression 'may be a predominantly individualistic event'. Is this supported?
options: Yes, it follows directly from the negative correlations reported in the results
No: individualism was never measured, so the claim doesn't follow from the data
Yes, because the sample was collected in one culture and so reflects its values
Yes, because the hypothesis was supported, which confirms the theory behind it
items.ans: No: individualism was never measured, so the claim doesn't follow from the data
items.model: Not supported by the data.
items.why: A conclusion must come from the results. This claim seems borrowed from other literature (e.g. Simpson et al., 1996).

items.label: Limitations stated
items.prompt: What TWO limitations do the authors list?
items.model: Small sample size; participants gave random answers.
items.why: Admitting participants answered randomly is serious: it questions the whole data set, yet they don't say how they dealt with it.

items.label: Limitation NOT mentioned
items.prompt: Name ONE important limitation the authors did NOT mention.
items.model: e.g. purposive sampling limits generalisability; correlation ≠ causation; self-report bias; no reliability data; no test comparing the groups; possible confounds (income, age, children).
items.why: Their limitations are thin. Spotting unstated limitations is a key critique skill.

items.label: Most relevant prior study
items.prompt: Most of the literature review is about teachers, students and the elderly. Which reviewed study is MOST directly related to working vs non-working women?
items.model: Hasnain, Ansari and Sethi (2011): working vs non-working (and married vs unmarried) women on life satisfaction and self-esteem.
items.why: A good literature review builds toward the gap. Here most studies are loosely related, and the gap is never clearly stated.

items.label: Ethics
items.prompt: What does the article report about ethics?
options: Ethics committee approval and written informed consent are both reported clearly
Only 'developing a good rapport'; no approval, consent or debriefing is mentioned
Only informed consent is mentioned; ethics approval and debriefing are left out
A full debriefing procedure is described, including referral for depressed women
items.ans: Only 'developing a good rapport'; no approval, consent or debriefing is mentioned
items.model: No ethics information.
items.why: Research with human participants should report approval and consent, especially with a sensitive measure like depression.
